title: Safe Reinforcement Learning with Preference-based Constraint Inference
one_liner: Learn safety rules from human rankings using a dead-zone gate that catches heavy-tailed risks humans worry about.
lead: Safe reinforcement learning means training a robot or system to follow both a reward goal and safety rules. The problem is that safety rules are messy and subjective—humans can say which action was less safe, but writing exact math formulas for safety is nearly impossible. This paper shows how to learn those messy safety rules from human feedback using a clever gate mechanism that catches the dangerous edge cases that standard feedback models miss.

problem.h2: Why do humans prefer some outcomes but ranking methods fail?
paras: When a robot learns from human feedback, we usually ask: which trajectory (a recorded sequence of states and actions) was better? A human watches two videos and ranks them, because ranking is much faster and cheaper than writing exact math formulas for safety. Standard models, like Bradley-Terry (BT) models, do exactly this ranking task: they learn to predict which option a human will prefer based on their rankings. This works fine for simple preferences.

But safety is different. Two trajectories might have the same ranking (both equally bad), yet one might pose a much greater risk because the dangerous event happens more often or with worse consequences. For instance, a robot might collide softly 5 times or collide hard once—both are ranked as bad, but one hides greater risk. Ranking models see both as equally bad and learn a constraint that is too loose, allowing unsafe behavior to slip through. The agent learns from this weak signal and fails to meet real safety limits.

callout.html: Preference models rank trajectories but ignore how concentrated the risk is. A heavy-tailed cost (rare, extreme events) looks identical to a light-tailed cost (many small events) in ranking because ranking only compares total cost, not the pattern of when costs occur, so the model underestimates how often the dangerous limit will be breached.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the cost prediction model
paras: Instead of a standard Bradley-Terry model (which ranks trajectories by total cost), this paper adds a dead-zone gate into the cost prediction network. The gate is a threshold: costs below the threshold get ignored (zero gradient), costs above it get pushed up. This simple gate makes the model learn from the extreme cases—the rare, dangerous scenarios that humans worry about—instead of being drowned out by the average.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: how often extreme costs appear
hidden.name: tail weight in the cost pattern
paras: The paper measures a hidden quantity that standard preference models ignore: how much the learned costs spike at the high end. In statistics, this is called a heavy tail—the probability of extreme costs is higher than a simple average would predict. A light-tailed distribution looks like a bell curve (most costs cluster at the middle). A heavy-tailed distribution looks like a hill with a long cliff on the right (a few extreme costs are much more likely than the formula suggests).

The dead-zone gate encourages the cost model to learn a heavier right tail. The paper proves this mathematically: Theorem 3.2 shows that over multiple training steps, the dead-zone loss accumulates stronger gradients for extreme costs, causing the learned distribution to have a strictly heavier right tail than a standard model. This tail weight is never named as a number—the paper infers it from the learned costs—but it is the reason the policy respects true safety.

heat.caption: Darker cells have higher estimated cost. Dead zone amplifies extreme costs (right side, marked).

reads.html: The dead-zone gate forces the model to focus on dangerous, rare outcomes. If most trajectories have low cost but a few have high cost, the gate ensures the high-cost ones dominate the learning signal because it amplifies their gradients (the directions the model learns), so the model predicts high expected cost for that type of scenario.

Lemma 3.1 proves the gradient advantage (the dead-zone loss has larger gradients for unsafe trajectories); Theorem 3.2 propagates this into multi-step dominance; Corollary 3.3 concludes that the learned cost distribution has a strictly heavier right tail than the standard loss.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the dead-zone gate amplifies dangerous signals
paras: The core mechanism is simple and mechanical. In a standard ranking model, the loss is a symmetric curve: a cost prediction that is too high or too low is equally penalized. The dead-zone gate breaks that symmetry. It says: if the cost is low, do not update (zero penalty). If the cost is high, penalize it just like before. This asymmetry forces the model to learn extreme costs in detail.

Why does this fix the problem? Because human preferences contain both common scenarios and rare, dangerous ones. A standard model averages over all scenarios equally. When the rare scenarios are extreme (high cost), they get diluted by the common, moderate scenarios. The dead-zone gate raises the cost of rare scenarios, so they carry more weight in the final expectation. The expected cumulative cost (which is what the constraint checks) rises, and the policy becomes more conservative to stay under the real limit.

The paper adds a second mechanism: a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) loss that encourages the cost model to predict high variance in cost estimates, which pushes the policy to explore uncertain regions and test the boundaries of safety. Together, the dead-zone gate (catches extremes) and SNR loss (explores uncertainty) build a cost model that respects real-world heavy-tailed risks.

stages.s: Preference pairs from humans (trajectory A ranked better than B) because humans can judge relative safety faster than specifying exact formulas
Assign cost scores via neural network
Dead-zone gate: ignore low costs, amplify high costs
SNR loss encourages variance in predictions
Cost model with heavy-tailed predictions, policy stays safe

math.words: The loss for the dead-zone safety term is zero when cost is below threshold, and grows quadratically when cost is above threshold, creating asymmetric gradients that amplify dangerous cases.
math.equation: L_DZ(cost) = 0 if cost <= d, else (cost - d)^2
symbols: the dead-zone threshold (boundary between safe and unsafe)
the dead-zone loss term (zero below threshold, quadratic above)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Safe trajectory: cost = 3. Loss = 0 (below threshold, no penalty).
Unsafe trajectory: cost = 8. Loss = (8 - 5)^2 = 9 (above threshold, penalized).
Unsafe trajectory: cost = 12. Loss = (12 - 5)^2 = 49 (further above, 5x harder penalty).
Gradient at cost=8 is 2*(8-5) = 6; at cost=12 is 2*(12-5) = 14. Model learns high costs much faster than low costs.

math.note: The dead-zone gate ignores safe costs and amplifies unsafe ones, so the neural network learns to predict higher costs for rare dangerous scenarios.

bars.h2: How much does it improve safety?

charts.title: Standard Bradley-Terry model
charts.note: Standard model focuses on ranking accuracy, not constraint alignment, so it underestimates rare risks.

charts.title: This paper (PbCRL with dead zone + SNR)
charts.note: Dead-zone gate catches extremes; policy learns honest costs; rare risks no longer hidden.

items.b: Dead zone set too high (threshold d too strict).
items.html: If the threshold is set above all realistic costs, the gate never activates, and the model reverts to standard ranking. No amplification of extremes, no safety gain.

items.b: Dead zone set too low (threshold d too lenient).
items.html: If the threshold is set below most costs, the gate amplifies common, benign scenarios as if they were dangerous. The policy becomes too conservative, sacrificing reward for false safety.
If humans only provide a few rankings, the pre-training phase cannot learn a good cost model. Fine-tuning will have to work harder and may still miss rare risks.

Humans provide a diverse set of preference rankings (including edge cases), the dead-zone threshold is calibrated to match the true safety limit, and SNR loss is weighted to encourage variance without noise. The model learns honest costs, policy respects constraints.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple robot navigation task (a 2D grid with obstacles and a goal). Assign a true safety constraint: the robot cannot spend more than a certain cumulative cost (e.g., collision penalties summed over all steps). Generate a dataset of 100 trajectory pairs ranked by humans (or synthetically, based on which avoids the high-cost obstacle). Train a standard Bradley-Terry model on the pairs, then train PbCRL (with dead-zone gate + SNR loss). Finally, run both learned policies on 50 test trajectories and measure how many times each policy violates the true safety constraint.
demo.metric_eq: constraint_violation_rate = (trajectories that exceed true cumulative cost limit) / (total test trajectories)
demo.closing: The demo succeeds if PbCRL's violation rate drops below 10% while the standard model stays above 25%, proving the dead-zone gate catches the rare, dangerous cases that ranking models miss.
